summary: Defines the Generic Security Service API, a common interface that applications use to get security services such as authentication, without being tied to one underlying security mechanism. It was a standards-track specification. It was replaced by RFC 2078.

plainLanguage.summary: Different locks need different keys, but this gives you one handle that works on all of them. Programs ask for security the same way no matter what is behind it.

questions: how does gss-api provide mechanism independence
what is a security context in gss-api
subtitle: A mechanism-independent interface for security services.

tldr.problem: Applications need strong authentication, integrity, and confidentiality services, but different systems use incompatible cryptographic technologies. Tying an application to one mechanism makes it unportable.
tldr.mechanism: GSS-API provides a common interface layer above underlying security mechanisms like Kerberos or X.509. Applications call standard GSS-API functions; the implementation selects which mechanism to use and handles the details.
tldr.outcome: Portable applications can authenticate users and protect messages without knowing which cryptographic mechanism is underneath, allowing the same code to run in different security environments.

today: RFC 1508 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 2078, which extends the API with additional features. The two-version approach reflects the evolution of GSS-API in response to deployment experience and the need for language-specific bindings.

sections.title: What Is GSS-API
sections.content:
The Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) is a language-independent specification for how applications ask for security services. It sits between application code and the cryptographic mechanisms that do the real work, allowing an application to authenticate users, establish shared secrets, and protect messages without needing to know which mechanism (Kerberos, X.509, or another) is actually being used.

The RFC defines the interface at a conceptual level independent of any programming language. Separate specifications describe how to bind these concepts to specific languages like C.
sections.plainLanguage: GSS-API is a translator between your program and the security system. Your program makes requests in the GSS-API language, and GSS-API translates them into whatever the underlying security system understands.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
GSS-API organizes its services around a few key constructs. A context is a pair of shared data structures, one at each end of a communication, that represent a security relationship between two peers. The context is established through an exchange of cryptographically protected tokens. Credentials give a process the right to act as a particular identity. Once a context exists, applications can use per-message operations to sign messages (providing authentication and integrity), seal them (adding optional encryption), or verify and unseal received messages.

A mechanism type identifies which underlying cryptographic technology is being used, such as Kerberos V5 or X.509. The RFC assumes both sides will agree on a mechanism and use it consistently across a context.
sections.plainLanguage: A context is a shared agreement between two programs: they've proven their identities and can now talk securely. A credential is a digital ID card that proves who you are. A token is the protected message used to set up the context.

sections.title: The Interface Calls
sections.content:
GSS-API provides three groups of operations. Credential management calls let applications acquire credentials, release them when done, or check what credentials they hold. Context-level calls establish and manage the security context: one side initiates with GSS_Init_sec_context(), the other accepts with GSS_Accept_sec_context(), and either side can delete the context or check how long it will remain valid.

Per-message calls protect individual messages once a context is established. GSS_Sign() and GSS_Verify() provide integrity and authentication without encryption. GSS_Seal() and GSS_Unseal() add optional confidentiality. The RFC also defines support calls for translating status codes to text, discovering which mechanisms are available, and working with names in a portable way.
sections.plainLanguage: The calls are like steps in a conversation: first you get proof of who you are (credentials), then both sides agree to trust each other (context), then you can send secure messages (per-message operations).

sections.title: Design Goals and Trade-offs
sections.content:
GSS-API was designed with four main goals. Mechanism independence means applications do not depend on a particular cryptographic approach. Protocol independence means GSS-API works with any communications protocol: TCP, UDP, RPC, or others. Protocol association independence means a single GSS-API implementation can be used by multiple protocol modules without conflicts. Finally, GSS-API can be used by applications whether or not they run within a trusted system boundary.

The RFC acknowledges design trade-offs. Replay detection and sequencing are optionally requested at context establishment time, since supporting them is resource-intensive. Quality-of-protection (QOP) parameters allow mechanisms to offer choices about the strength of protection, but callers can request a default and remain portable.
sections.plainLanguage: GSS-API tries to be useful in many situations: different cryptography systems, different network protocols, different program structures. But it keeps things simple by letting you choose defaults and only tweak details when you need to.

sections.title: Status Reporting and Error Handling
sections.content:
Every GSS-API call returns two status values. A major_status code gives a mechanism-independent indication of success or failure: GSS_COMPLETE means success, GSS_CONTINUE_NEEDED means another call is needed (for multi-step exchanges), and various error codes indicate what went wrong. A minor_status code provides additional mechanism-specific detail about errors.

This dual-status design allows callers to control their flow based on standardized outcomes while underlying mechanisms can report precise errors. Status codes are defined to be mechanism-independent so that applications can handle success and common errors uniformly.
sections.plainLanguage: Each call tells you two things: a general answer (did it work?), and a specific detail (why or how). The general answer is the same for all security systems, but the detail can vary.
